Fantastic is my own harness. It runs on an Erlang-like, OS-like meta-runtime instead of agent loops or agent graphs.

I believe this is the right design for an AI runtime: it puts humans, AI agents and tools on equal footing.

It will grow into a convenient multi-OS runtime that can do what other AI libraries and harnesses do. For now it’s a technical demo with two modes: a CLI coder, and a spatial canvas that’s very handy for a lot of everyday work.

I think the canvas mode is the kind of software we’ll all be using in the 2030s.

I don’t have a name for it yet, so for now let’s call it “emergent software”. The idea is that you build, run and engineer your own systems visually, with help from AI, inside your own dynamic interface that you build for yourself. It’s a lot of fun, especially for multimedia projects.

For example, in a canvas project I’m still working on, a third-party AI agent generates UI and agents: it builds a control panel for making a Manim animation, and a viewport for a Blender video built from the Manim animation’s guidelines. Having rare-earth minerals is one thing, being able to extract and separate the rare-earth metals from their minerals is a completely different thing.

For now, China has a huge advantage in the facilities for the chemical processing of the rare-earth minerals, so that much of what is mined elsewhere still goes to China for the extraction and separation of the metals.

Some rare-earth metals are very cheap, like cerium and lanthanum. Even neodymium is not expensive. Unfortunately most applications also need at least small quantities of those rare-earth elements that are really rare, i.e. they form a very small fraction of the rare-earth elements contained in a mineral, and whose separation from the abundant rare-earth elements is also very expensive.

So this phrase that is too often repeated "Rare earths are not as rare as the name suggests" is actually false for most of the 14 REEs. Not rare are only lanthanum, cerium and neodymium, which cover only a small part of the applications of REEs, like deoxidizers in metallurgy and glass polishing and lighters. Most magnets with neodymium must also include other much less abundant rare-earth metals, to increase their upper limit for the working temperature.
